As an eighth grade student, I believe that requiring community service or extra punishment for students who violate school regulations is an effective way to promote positive behavior and a sense of responsibility among students. In this essay, I will research and compare the benefits of each approach and analyze their impact on students and the school community.

Community service is an approach that requires students to perform volunteer work in their community as a form of punishment for breaking school rules. This approach has several benefits for both the students and the school community. Firstly, community service provides students with an opportunity to give back to their community and develop a sense of empathy and compassion for others. This can help to reduce the likelihood of future rVlebreaking behavior, as students become more aware of the impact their actions have on others.

Secondly, community service can help to improve students' social skills and sense of belonging. By working with other volunteers, students can learn to communicate effectively, work collaboratively, and build relationships with people from different backgrounds. This can help to foster a sense of community and reduce feelings of isolation or exclusion that may contribute to rVlebreaking behavior.

On the other hand, extra punishment, such as detention or suspension, is another approach that can be Used to deter students from breaking school rules. While this approach may be effective in the short term, it can have negative consequences for both the students and the school community. For example, students who are punished excessively may become resentful or feel Unfairly targeted, which can lead to further rVlebreaking behavior or even dropout.

Additionally, extra punishment can create a culture of punishment and retribution within the school community, which can Undermine the positive relationships and trust that are necessary for a successful learning environment. This can lead to a cycle of negative behavior, where students feel more and more isolated and disengaged, and are less likely to succeed academically or socially.

In conclusion, I believe that community service is the more effective approach for promoting positive behavior and a sense of responsibility among students. This approach provides students with an opportunity to give back to their community, develop empathy and compassion, and improve their social skills. On the other hand, extra punishment can have negative consequences for both the students and the school community, and can create a culture of punishment and retribution.

Overall, limiting car usage has several advantages, including the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, reduced congestion, improved air quality, and the promotion of alternative and sustainable transportation options. In addition, limiting car usage can help to improve public health. Walking and biking are both good forms of exercise, and they can help to reduce obesity and other health problems. By encouraging people to walk or bike instead of driving, we can help to improve the health of our communities.

Finally, limiting car usage can help to save money. Car ownership is a major expense, and it can be difficult for people to afford both a car and the associated costs of insurance, gas, and parking. By limiting car usage, we can save money on these costs and free up resources that can be used for other purposes.

In conclusion, there are a number of advantages to limiting car usage. By reducing air pollution, traffic congestion, and the number of accidents, we can make our communities cleaner, safer, and healthier. We can also save money and improve our quality of life.

By making public transportation more convenient and affordable, we can encourage people to use it instead of driving. We can also make our cities more walkable and bikeable by building more sidewalks and bike lanes. And we can educate people about the benefits of limiting car usage.

Limiting car usage is a challenge, but it is one that is worth pursuing. By making a few changes to the way we live, we can make our communities cleaner, safer, and healthier.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to you today to express my support for abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President of the United States by popular vote.

The Electoral College is an outdated system that is no longer reflective of the will of the people. In the last five presidential elections, the candidate who won the popular vote has lost the election twice. This is simply not acceptable in a democracy.

The Electoral College was created at a time when the United States was a very different country. At the time, there were only 13 states in the Union, and travel and communication were much more difficult than they are today. The Electoral College was designed to give more power to the smaller states, which were concerned that they would be ignored by the larger states.

However, the United States has changed dramatically since the Electoral College was created. There are now 50 states, and travel and communication are much easier. The Electoral College is no longer necessary to protect the interests of the smaller states.

In fact, the Electoral College actually works against the interests of the smaller states. Because of the winner-take-all system, candidates can focus their attention on a handful of "battleground" states and ignore the rest of the country. This means that the votes of people in many states are essentially meaningless.

The Electoral College also leads to voter suppression. In states with a winner-take-all system, people who live in a state that is heavily in favor of one party may feel like their vote doesn't matter. This can discourage them from voting, which is a serious problem in a democracy.

I believe that the best way to ensure that the President is elected by the will of the people is to abolish the Electoral College and elect the President by popular vote. This would give every American citizen an equal voice in the election, and it would ensure that the President is accountable to the entire country.

I urge you to support abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President by popular vote. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,

Subject: In Favor of Keeping the Electoral College

Dear Senator [Senator's Last Name],

I am writing to express my support for the Electoral College and urge you to consider the benefits it provides in our presidential elections. While some argue for a change to a popular vote system, I believe that maintaining the Electoral College is crucial for several reasons.

Firstly, the Electoral College ensures certainty of outcome in our elections. In a popular vote system, disputes over the election outcome are more likely to occur, as the winner may only have a slight plurality of votes. On the other hand, the Electoral College system ensures that the winning candidate's share of the electoral votes exceeds their share of the popular vote. This reduces the chances of disputes and provides a clear winner for the presidency.

Additionally, the Electoral College promotes a sense of unity and representation for all regions of the country. With this system, presidential candidates are required to have trans-regional appeal and cannot solely rely on winning one region. This encourages candidates to campaign in all states and address the concerns of diverse populations, rather than focusing solely on populous areas. It ensures that the president represents the interests of citizens from all regions, rather than just a few.

Moreover, the role of swing states in the Electoral College system encourages voter attentiveness and thoughtful decision-making. Toss-up states, in which the outcome is uncertain, receive much attention and resources from candidates. This results in voters in these states being more engaged and informed about the political campaigns, as they ultimately decide the election. By giving these voters a significant say in the outcome, we ensure that the most thoughtful and informed electorate decides who becomes president.

The Electoral College also provides balance and attention to all states, regardless of their size and population. Large states may lose some weight in the political balance due to the mal-apportionment of the Senate, but the Electoral College restores some of this balance. Presidential candidates are incentivized to campaign in large states, ensuring that the concerns and issues of these states are addressed. This ensures that the interests of all states are considered in the election process.

Lastly, the Electoral College eliminates the need for run-off elections, which can complicate the presidential election process. In situations where no candidate receives a majority of the popular vote, the Electoral College consistently produces a clear winner. This allows for a smooth and efficient transition of power, saving time and resources that would otherwise be utilized in further elections.

While some argue that the Electoral College may discourage voters in states where their preferred candidate has no chance of winning, the data shows that voter turnout remains high in presidential elections. Voters participate in the process to express their political preferences and engage in the democratic system, rather than solely with the hopes of swinging a national election. Therefore, the Electoral College system does not hinder voter participation significantly.

In conclusion, the Electoral College plays a vital role in our presidential elections and should be preserved. It ensures certainty of outcome, promotes unity and representation for all regions, encourages thoughtful voter engagement, provides balance to all states, and avoids the complexities of run-off elections. These benefits make the Electoral College an important part of our democratic process.

Thank you for considering my perspective on this matter. I trust that you will make an informed decision that upholds the principles of our democracy and best serves the interests of our great nation. I appreciate your attention to this issue and look forward to hearing about your stance on the Electoral College.

Yours sincerely,

In recent years, there has been a growing trend in Europe, the United States, and other parts of the world to separate suburban life from auto use. This shift is part of a broader movement called "smart planning," which seeks to make cities and towns more accessible to public transportation, with less space for parking. The advantages of limiting car usage are numerous, including reduced greenhouse gas emissions, improved air and water quality, increased public safety, and enhanced livability.

One of the most significant advantages of limiting car usage is the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. In Europe, transportation accounts for 12% of total greenhouse gas emissions, and up to 50% in some car intensive areas in the United States. By reducing reliance on cars, cities can significantly decrease their carbon footprint. This is achieved by promoting alternative modes of transportation such as walking, cycling, public transit, and car sharing.

In addition to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, limiting car usage can also improve air and water quality. Cars emit harmful pollutants such as nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, and volatile organic compounds, which can have negative effects on human health and the environment. By reducing car usage, cities can lower these pollutant levels, resulting in cleaner air and water.

Another advantage of limiting car usage is increased public safety. Cars, especially those operated by inexperienced or impaired drivers, can be dangerous. By reducing the number of cars on the road, cities can reduce accidents and improve overall road safety.

Furthermore, reducing car usage can enhance livability in cities. With less traffic and noise, streets become more walkable and bike friendly, creating a more vibrant and connected community. Pedestrians and cyclists are also exposed to more fresh air and sunshine, which can lead to better health outcomes.

Despite these advantages, there are some counterclaims to limiting car usage. One concern is that reducing car usage could lead to an increase in public transportation use, resulting in overcrowding and longer commute times. However, research suggests that by improving the quality and efficiency of public transportation systems, cities can reduce congestion and make them more attractive to commuters.

Title: Exploring Venus

Introduction

Venus is the second planet from the sun, and it's often referred to as Earth's "sister planet." Venus is unique in its own way due to its atmosphere, geological features, and extreme temperatures. Over the years, various space probes have been sent to explore Venus, allowing us to gather valuable information about this fascinating world. In this essay, we'll discuss some key discoveries made by these missions, focusing on its atmosphere, geology, and climate.
Atmosphere
The atmosphere of Venus is composed mostly of carbon dioxide, with clouds of sulfuric acid forming its thick layer of clouds that cover the entire planet. These clouds are so dense that they block most sunlight from reaching the surface, making it difficult to study Venus' surface features from space. The high atmospheric pressure on Venus is also extreme, being over 90 times that of Earth's. These conditions have made it difficult for spacecraft to survive on the planet's surface for long.
Geology and Surface Features
Venus has a unique landscape characterized by volcanic plains and mountains. It has no active volcanoes, but it has numerous extinct volcanoes. The planet is also known for having a large number of impact craters. One of the most significant geological features on Venus is a network of tesserae, which are large, flat-topped mountains with steep slopes. These mountains are believed to be the result of tectonic activity and volcanic processes that occurred billions of years ago.
Extreme Temperatures and Climate
The extreme conditions on Venus make it difficult for life as we know it to exist. Its surface temperature can reach up to 864 degrees Fahrenheit (462 degrees Celsius), hot enough to melt lead. This extreme heat is a result of the greenhouse effect, where the thick atmosphere traps heat from the sun, causing Venus to have a runaway greenhouse effect. The planet's atmosphere also contains a small percentage of carbon monoxide, which contributes to the overall warming.
Conclusion
In conclusion, Venus is an enigmatic planet filled with unique geological features and extreme conditions. While it may not be a suitable place for human life as we know it, it continues to fascinate scientists with its complex atmosphere, geology, and extreme temperature. As more space probes are sent to explore Venus, our understanding of this mysterious planet will undoubtedly grow.

For these reasons it is important for high school students to start thinking about their future career.

Title: Embracing Car-Free Cities: A Sustainable Future for Urban Living

Introduction:
Cities around the world are becoming more congested and polluted as a result of increasing motor vehicle use. To address this issue and promote sustainability, some cities are transitioning towards becoming car-free zones. In this essay, I will discuss the concept of car-free cities, their benefits, and the challenges they face.

Benefits of Car-Free Cities:
1. Reduced Air Pollution: With fewer vehicles on the road, there is less emission of harmful pollutants, such as greenhouse gases and particulate matter, which improve air quality in urban areas.
2. Improved Public Health: As a result of cleaner air, residents living in car-free cities experience better overall health.
3. Enhanced Safety: Eliminating cars from the streets reduces the risk of traffic accidents, especially for pedestrians and cyclists.
4. Increased Physical Activity: Car-free cities encourage residents to use alternative forms of transportation, such as cycling, walking, or using public transportation, leading to more physical activity and a healthier lifestyle.
5. Improved Urban Design: By prioritizing pedestrians and cyclists over cars, cities become more pedestrian-friendly and promote social interactions.
6. Reduced Noise Pollution: Fewer cars on the streets mean less noise pollution in urban areas, providing a more peaceful environment for residents to live, work, and play.
7. Environmental Sustainability: Eliminating or reducing the need for private vehicles contributes to a lower carbon footprint and helps cities meet their climate goals.
8. Economic Benefits: With fewer cars on the road, cities can save money on infrastructure and maintenance costs, as well as reduce congestion, which leads to increased productivity and economic activity.

Challenges for Car-Free Cities:
1. Infrastructure Development: To successfully transition to a car-free city, cities need to have well-designed and maintained infrastructure for alternative modes of transportation, such as bike lanes, walking paths, and public transportation.
2. Cultural Acceptance: Residents may face challenges in adapting to a car-free lifestyle, as they have grown accustomed to relying on personal vehicles for transportation.
3. Economic Inequality: Car-free cities may not be feasible or accessible for low-income individuals who rely on cars to access essential services or jobs.
4. Logistical Concerns: Ensuring the smooth operation of public transportation systems, maintaining adequate parking facilities for non-residents, managing delivery services, and accommodating visitors can be complex and costly.

Conclusion:
Car-free cities offer numerous benefits in terms of improved public health, reduced pollution, enhanced safety, and promoting sustainability. However, they also face challenges such as infrastructure development, cultural acceptance, and economic inequality. To make car-free cities a reality, cities must address these challenges and work together towards a more sustainable, healthier urban future

The Electoral College is a unique aspect of the United States' presidential election process, which raises concerns about its effectiveness in accurately selecting the presidential candidate who best represents the American people's interests.

The primary argument against the Electoral College is that it undermines the concept of "one person, one vote." In a democratic society, every citizen's vote should count equally; however, in the Electoral College system, a voter in a less populous state may have a disproportionate effect on electing a president due to the distribution of electoral votes.
Additionally, the Electoral College has the potential to cause "winner-takes-all" outcomes in states where one candidate wins a majority, while the other candidate garners a significant minority. This can lead to a candidate receiving the necessary electoral votes without a majority of the popular vote.
Furthermore, the Electoral College can be susceptible to manipulation by political parties. For instance, strategic campaigning in certain states can lead to candidates focusing on a smaller number of swing states rather than the entire country. This can result in a situation where the president is elected by a minority of states.
However, the Electoral College does have its merits. It serves as a safeguard against the potential tyranny of the majority, ensuring that smaller states have a voice in the presidential election process. It also helps to maintain a federalist system, where states have a degree of autonomy in decision-making.
In conclusion, the effectiveness of the Electoral College is debatable. While it has its advantages, such as preserving the voices of smaller states, it also poses issues like undermining the concept of "one person, one vote," and the potential for manipulation and "winner-takes-all" outcomes. The question remains: does the Electoral College work? The answer lies within the balance between preserving states' rights and ensuring a fair and equitable presidential election process.

To fully comprehend the significance of a Facial Action Coding System or FACS, one must delve into the realm of facial expressions and their connection to human emotions and language. The study of facial expressions and their interpretations is rooted in the foundations of psychology, anthropology, and communication sciences. It is a multidisciplinary field that seeks to understand various aspects of nonverbal communication.

The Facial Action Coding System was first conceived and developed by renowned American psychologist Paul Ekman, along with Wallace V. Friesen, an anatomist, and colleague, and Wallace V. Moyer, a computer scientist. This groundbreaking model revolutionized the study of facial expressions and emotion, serving as a fundamental tool to disentangle the relationship between emotions, expressions, and their underlying body movements.

FACS is composed of a series of action units or motor movements that can be observed on the human face while expressing emotions and responding to specific stimuli. It is a systematically developed, precise, and consistent way to represent the complex facial movements involved in emotional expression. It provides a framework to decode how a person looks when they feel an emotion or experience a particular state of mind. These action units are universal, being used by various cultures and individuals worldwide despite language, gender, or race boundaries.

The basic building blocks of FACS are the action units, which are named and numbered sequentially. There are a total of 46 action units described in the system. These action units can be simple or compound. Simple action units involve movement in a single anatomical region, like raising an eyebrow or froming, while compound action units are combinations of two or more simple action units or movements. For instance, a smile can involve both an elevation of the corners of the mouth (action unit AU12) and elevation of the cheeks (auction unit AU10), both of which are components of complex or compound action units.

The FACS framework has been particularly useful in multiple disciplines, such as psychology, linguistics, neuroscience, and education. Psychologists can use the system to study human emotion, explore how it relates to personality traits, or analyze facial signals in interactions between people. The FACS can also help in understanding cultural differences in expressing emotions and facial expressions, as it provides a neutral categorization system for universal action units.

In linguistics, the FACS theory has facilitated research into the relationship between face and language. The analysis of facial movements can offer an insight into the origins and development of particular languages or investigate the connection between emotional expression and the language we use. For instance, studies have found that certain emotions displayed through facial expressions may predict the likelihood of specific linguistic constructions in conversation.

The neuroscience domain has been a major beneficiary of the implementation of FACS, with research focusing on decoding human consciousness and understanding how different neural mechanisms underlie emotional expression and decision-making. The use of FACS has helped reveal the intricate relationship between facial movements and brain activity during emotions and other emotional experiences. For example, understanding how our facial movements respond to specific emotions can aid in recognizing brain processes involved in emotional regulation, a key factor in neurological research.

In the field of education, FACS has played a vital role in enhancing emotional intelligence and social-emotional learning amongst students. Educators can utilize the system to facilitate better communication skills, identify emotions in various contexts, and teach non-verbal cues. By encouraging students to recognize and reflect upon their facial expressions while working with others, schools and teachers foster emotional awareness and empathy.

Moreover, FACS has found applications in forensic science, clinical settings, and even in the entertainment industry. In crime investigation, it plays a vital role by helping experts decode subtle expressions displayed by suspects during interviews and interrogations. In medical applications, it aids clinicians in diagnosing neurological and psychiatric conditions, as well as monitor treatment responses and determine the severity of injuries or diseases through facial muscle activity. Meanwhile, in the entertainment world, FACS has been utilized in the development of animations, as artists can better depict emotional states and gestures in their characters.

In conclusion, the Facial Action Coding System represents an essential tool in the study of emotions, expressions, and communication. By providing a systematic approach to facial movements and their emotional correlates, it has become an essential framework for various research fields. When faced with an important decision, it is wise to gather perspectives from different people. No single person can possibly have all the answers or consider every angle of a complex situation. Getting advice from multiple trusted sources helps you develop a more well rounded understanding of your options and their potential consequences. 

For example, let's say a student is deciding whether to pursue music or science in college. They may talk to a parent, teacher, family friend, and older sibling. Each person likely has a different background and life experiences that shape their point of view. The parent may emphasize career stability and financial security, while the music teacher highlights the student's passion and talent. A science minded family friend could discuss opportunities in fields like acoustical engineering. Hearing these varied perspectives exposes the student to angles they may not have considered alone. 

Seeking multiple opinions also protects against bias. Any one person may be inclined to push their own agenda or have a blind spot that skews their advice. But getting several perspectives helps balance out those individual biases or blind spots. The varied views can highlight objectively better choices rather than just reflecting what appeals most to a single adviser. No one adviser has a monopoly on truth or the full scope of considerations. 

Finally, mulling over different counsel expands one's thinking beyond initial impressions. What seemed like the obvious right answer from just one person's counsel may look more complex or uncertain when weighed against other rational considerations. The process of actively comparing disparate advice and forming one's own conclusion breeds stronger critical thinking skills. It empowers the person seeking counsel to make the choice most right for their own unique situation and priorities, not just someone else's perspective. 

In summary, making big decisions is challenging. Talking to more than one trusted source provides a well rounded picture, protects against bias, and encourages independent thought all of which can lead to choosing the option that truly is the best personal fit rather than just seeming best from a single limited viewpoint. Gathering multiple perspectives is wise advice indeed when making life's important choices.

While cell phones have become an integral part of modern life, they can create serious safety issues when used while driving. For this reason, drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity when operating a vehicle.

There are several reasons' cell phone use by drivers should be prohibited. First and foremost is the danger of distracted driving. When talking or texting on a phone, a driver's attention is split between operating the vehicle and the phone conversation or texts. Numerous studies have shown that even hands-free phone use can be distracting. This puts not only the driver at risk, but also endangers other motorists and pedestrians sharing the road.

Distracted driving from cell phone use has been linked to an alarming number of car accidents. According to the National Safety Council, over 25% of all car crashes involve cell phone use. Texting while driving in particular makes an accident over 20 times more likely. With so much at stake, it is simply not worth the risk to allow any kind of cell phone function behind the wheel.

In addition, cell phone conversations may slow a driver's reaction time. Having to focus attention on a phone call rather than the road ahead delays the processing of visual and audio cues needed for safe motor vehicle operation. A two second delay in braking or steering could mean the difference between a near miss and a serious accident. 

Many developed nations and states within the U.S. already ban handheld and hand free cell phone use for drivers. The research clearly shows prohibiting any cell phone function for drivers is the prudent choice to enhance roadway safety. With human lives on the line each time someone gets behind the wheel, the small sacrifice of not using a phone is well worth reducing preventable accidents. For the protection of all people who share the roads, drivers must be fully focused on their primary responsibility operating their vehicles safely.

The Importance of the Electoral College in Presidential Elections

Dear Senator [Senator's Last Name],

I am writing to express my support for the Electoral College and urge you to consider the benefits it brings to our democratic process. While some argue for a shift to a popular vote system, I believe that maintaining the Electoral College is crucial for ensuring a fair and balanced representation of the diverse interests of all states.

The Electoral College, as established by our founding fathers, serves as a compromise between election of the President by Congress or a purely popular vote. It consists of 538 electors, with a majority of 270 electoral votes required to win the presidency. The selection of electors is made by the states based on their Congressional representation, ensuring that smaller states have a voice in the election process. 

One of the main advantages of the Electoral College is the certainty of outcome it provides. A dispute over the popular vote is more likely to occur than a dispute over the Electoral College's results. The winnertakeall system in most states contributes to this certainty, as even a slight plurality in a state leads to a landslide electoral vote victory. Additionally, the Electoral College avoids the issue of runoff elections, as it invariably produces a clear winner.

Furthermore, the Electoral College fosters the election of a president who has transregional appeal. With no region having enough electoral votes to secure a victory, candidates must have broad appeal across different regions of the country. This requirement ensures that the president represents all regions and prioritizes the interests of all Americans, not just a particular region.

The Electoral College system also places attention on swing states, where campaign efforts are concentrated. This focus on key states increases voter engagement in those states and encourages voters to thoroughly evaluate the candidates and their policies. By giving more power to swing states, we ensure that thoughtful and well informed voters have a greater influence on the outcome of the election.

Moreover, the Electoral College balances the political weight between large and small states. While the Senate already provides some balance through apportionment, the Electoral College further emphasizes the importance of large states in the political process. Candidates are compelled to pay attention to these states due to their higher number of electoral votes, granting citizens in large states a fair share of influence in presidential elections.

Lastly, abolishing the Electoral College would undermine the representation of states with smaller populations, and candidates would focus solely on populous regions and disregard the concerns of less populated areas. This could exacerbate divisions between urban and rural areas and lead to a concentration of power in heavily populated regions. The Electoral College ensures that the interests of all states, regardless of population size, are taken into account during presidential elections.

In conclusion, the Electoral College remains a critical component of our democratic system, striking a delicate balance between the popular vote and the interests of states. It guarantees a certainty of outcome, promotes transregional appeal, encourages voter engagement in swing states, provides balance between large and small states, and avoids runoff elections. I respectfully request that you consider the benefits outlined above when making decisions regarding the Electoral College.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. I trust that you will take my viewpoint into consideration when evaluating any potential changes to our presidential election process.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]

I agree that students should not memorize facts without understanding the ideas, trends, and concepts that help explain those facts. In the modern world, knowledge is essential. However, it is not just facts that are important, but also the ability to think critically and make connections between different pieces of information. Memorizing facts without understanding the ideas, trends, and concepts behind them does not help students develop this essential skill of critical thinking. Rather, it encourages rote memorization, which is not a useful task if the goal is to foster understanding.

For example, in a history class, a student might memorize the date of the Civil War, but without understanding the economic and political tensions of the time, they would not be able to understand why the war happened or what the ramifications were. Understanding the context of a particular fact is essential for being able to make connections between different ideas, form useful arguments, and make decisions.

In addition, memorizing facts without understanding the ideas, trends, and concepts behind them is a time consuming and inefficient way to learn. Memorizing facts requires a lot of repetition and dedication, but it does not lead to true learning or understanding. On the other hand, if students take the time to understand the ideas, trends, and concepts behind facts, they can more easily apply that knowledge to future situations and problems. For example, if a student is presented with a problem in a math class, they can draw on their understanding of the underlying concepts to come up with a solution, rather than having to look up the answer in a book.

Ultimately, memorizing facts without understanding the ideas, trends, and concepts behind them is not a productive or efficient use of time. Students who take the time to understand the context of facts are more likely to be able to make connections between different pieces of information, which will be essential for their success in any field.

Title: Advantages of Limiting Car Usage: Lessons from Global Experiments

The twenty first century has seen a burgeoning interest in creating sustainable communities around the world. One common thread in this endeavor is the effort to limit car usage in suburban areas, thereby reducing greenhouse gas emissions. This essay features examples from Vauban, Germany; Paris, France; Bogota, Colombia; and the United States, cited from articles by Elisabeth Rosenthal, Robert Duffer, and Andrew Silky.

Vauban, a German suburb, provides an illustrative example of a near carefree community. As noted by Elisabeth Rosenthal, Vauban's layout substantially limits street parking, home garages, and driveways, resulting in 70% of families not owning cars. Vauban has made strides in aligning suburban life with sustainable environmental norms through a strategy known as "smart planning" (Rosenthal, 2009). The community’s architecture favors pedestrians and cyclists, while the scarce parking options disincentivize car ownership.

Paris, on the other hand, sought to combat record level pollution by implementing a temporary driving ban (Duffer, 2014). The tactic yielded an apparent drop in pollution levels, underscoring the direct correlation between car usage and air quality deterioration. The strategy's success signals a potential approach for other highly polluted cities worldwide.

Meanwhile, Bogota, Colombia, has added a dimension to the discourse through its annual "Day Without Cars." In promoting pedestrian friendly infrastructures and gaining widespread participation, this event strongly advocates for alternative means of transportation as a solution to reducing pollution and providing stress relief for citizens (Silky, 2002).

In the United States, the trend of peak driving seems to be on the decline, with Americans—particularly younger generations—showing less interest in owning cars (Rosenthal, 2013). This shift, influenced by factors such as technological advancements and urban renewal, has positive implications for greenhouse gas emissions. However, this trend could prove problematic for the auto industry, encouraging companies like Ford and Mercedes to reimagine themselves as “mobility” companies.

In summary, limiting car usage offers the distinct advantage of reduced greenhouse gas emissions, leading to cleaner air and a healthier environment. Notably, it is not just about less driving but intelligent urban planning. In encouraging pedestrian friendly infrastructure, cities can foster a community less dependent on personal vehicles. A collective transition can make cities everywhere more sustainable, liveable spaces for all residents. Thus, it seems that reducing car dependence is a necessity for wisely managing our planet's resources against the mounting threat of climate change.

The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is a groundbreaking technology that has the potential to revolutionize the way teachers connect with their students in the classroom. This software uses the digital window into the human psyche to interpret the subtlest of facial expressions and identify a range of emotions. As a 10th-grade student, I believe that the use of this technology to read the emotional expressions of students is valuable and can positively impact the educational experience.

Firstly, the FACS technology offers a real-time emotional map of the classroom, empowering teachers to tailor their approach to individual student needs. This means that teachers can recognize when a student is confused, bored, or interested, and adjust their teaching methods accordingly. For example, if a student is struggling to understand a concept, the teacher can provide additional support or explain it in a different way to help the student comprehend better. This personalized approach to learning can lead to better engagement, motivation, and ultimately, academic success.

Secondly, the FACS technology can differentiate between confusion and boredom, between interest and indifference, offering educators a tool not just for understanding but for engagement and intervention. This means that teachers can identify when a student is losing interest in a topic and intervene to make the lesson more engaging. For instance, if a student is showing signs of boredom, the teacher can introduce a new activity or discussion to make the lesson more interactive and interesting. This can help to keep students motivated and engaged in their learning.

Thirdly, the FACS technology can adapt lessons in real-time, just like an effective human instructor. This means that teachers can focus their attention where it's most needed, while the software ensures that each student's learning journey is as individual as they are. For example, if a student is struggling with a particular concept, the software can adapt the lesson to provide additional support and resources to help the student understand better. This personalized approach to learning can lead to better academic outcomes and increased student satisfaction.

Furthermore, the FACS technology fosters a sense of community and mutual understanding among students. Recognizing that facial expressions are universal, the system helps students see that they are not alone in their emotional responses. This shared understanding can foster collaboration and empathy, breaking down barriers of isolation and misunderstanding. For instance, if a student is feeling anxious or stressed, the software can identify these emotions and provide resources to help the student manage their emotions. This can create a supportive and inclusive learning environment that promotes social and emotional learning.

However, some skeptics may argue that the FACS technology may not be effective in understanding complex human emotions and the nuances of face-to-face learning. They may also argue that the software may replace human interaction, which is essential for student learning. But as Dr. Huang points out, much of human communication is nonverbal, and the software isn't replacing human interaction; it's enhancing it. The FACS technology provides teachers with additional tools to understand and support their students, rather than replacing human interaction altogether.

In conclusion, the use of the Facial Action Coding System to read the emotional expressions of students in a classroom is valuable. This technology offers a real-time emotional map of the classroom, differentiates between various emotions, adapts lessons in real-time, and fosters a sense of community and mutual understanding among students. While some may have concerns about the efficacy of this technology, I believe that it has the potential to revolutionize the way teachers connect with their students and promote a positive and inclusive learning environment.

Seeking input from multiple people when facing an important decision or choice is often wise because it allows you to gain different perspectives. No single person has all the answers or sees things from every angle, so hearing varying viewpoints can provide valuable insights. 

Different people have had different experiences that shape how they think about issues. Their backgrounds, areas of expertise, personalities, and life circumstances all play a role in the advice they give. Getting opinions from individuals with diverse backgrounds therefore exposes you to considerations you might otherwise overlook if only talking to one person. For a major decision like choosing a career path or college, taking the time to discuss your options with people in different careers or alma maters could reveal important factors to weigh that a single adviser may not bring up.

Additionally, other people may notice strengths or weaknesses in various choices that you are too close to see objectively yourself. When your judgment is clouded by emotion or personal biases related to an issue, an outside perspective can help provide a more balanced look at your alternatives. People further removed from the situation may also spot potential pitfalls that you did not foresee but need to plan for. For example, friends and family helped one high school student analyze the pros and cons of both community college and a four-year university to better determine the right starting point after graduation.  

Seeking multiple viewpoints also decreases the chance that you will make a choice solely based on faulty or incomplete information from one source. If different advisers present conflicting information, it alerts you to take a closer look to determine what is really accurate. And getting several advice-givers to help think through a dilemma from all angles helps safeguard against relying on advice that overlooks key considerations or fails to fully explore viable alternatives. The more well-rounded understanding of a decision that comes from canvassing various trusted sources reduces risk and increases confidence that your ultimate choice is based on the soundest rationale.

In summary, carefully considering counsel from multiple respected sources enables more informed decision-making. Exposure to an array of perspectives and life experiences prevents tunnel vision and catches potential flaws or oversights that any single opinion may contain. Such diligence in seeking diverse viewpoints helps ensure the choice that feels best reflects a comprehensive evaluation of all important factors.

Driverless cars, also known as autonomous vehicles, have been a fascinating subject of discussion among both the general public and experts in the field of transportation. The idea of a car that can drive itself seems to be something straight out of a science fiction movie. However, it's a rapidly advancing technology with the potential to transform the way people travel in the future.
One of the most significant advantages of driverless cars is their ability to improve road safety. Accidents occur due to human error, whether it be from distractions, impaired judgments, or simple mistakes. By removing human drivers, autonomous vehicles eliminate these risks, as they are designed to make decisions based on data collected from sensors and advanced algorithms.
Moreover, driverless cars can significantly improve traffic flow and reduce congestion on roads. With the help of artificial intelligence, these vehicles can communicate with each other, optimizing their routes to minimize travel time and avoiding accidents by anticipating other cars' actions.
Additionally, these cars have the potential to provide transportation for those who are unable to drive themselves, such as the elderly or disabled. By providing an affordable and convenient option, autonomous vehicles can significantly improve their quality of life.
Furthermore, driverless cars have the potential to decrease our dependence on fossil fuels and promote sustainable transportation. With improved fuel efficiency and the possibility of using renewable energy sources to power these vehicles, they can reduce greenhouse gas emissions and contribute to a cleaner environment. This could lead to a significant reduction in the negative impact on our environment.
Despite the many benefits of driverless cars, there are still concerns that need to be addressed. One such concern is the potential job loss for professional drivers, as driverless cars would eliminate the need for human drivers. However, it's crucial to note that new job opportunities may emerge in fields like software development, maintenance, and customer service related to autonomous vehicles.
Moreover, there are questions surrounding the security and privacy of driverless cars. Cybersecurity concerns arise due to the potential vulnerability of connected vehicles. Additionally, the data collected by the cars may raise privacy concerns.
Another concern is the potential for accidents involving driverless cars. Although these cars are designed to minimize the risk of accidents, there is always a chance of unexpected situations, and the responsibility for these accidents could be difficult to determine.
In conclusion, while driverless cars have the potential to revolutionize the way people travel, there are still many issues that must be addressed before they can become mainstream. It's crucial to ensure the technology is safe, secure, and privacy-conscious. However, the benefits of reduced road accidents, improved traffic flow, and sustainability make autonomous vehicles an exciting and promising innovation that has the potential to transform our transportation system in the future.

The Pursuit of Knowledge: Evaluating the Risks of Exploring Venus

The pursuit of scientific discovery often requires taking risks, yet the potential rewards of new knowledge make facing dangers worthwhile according to many explorers and scientists. In the article "The Challenge of Exploring Venus," the author argues that studying Venus through orbital missions and potential surface missions is a noble goal worth attempting despite the significant hazards the planet presents. Overall, the author builds a compelling case that learning about Earth's closest planetary neighbor merits facing risks due to the still unknown details Venus could reveal about the formation of terrestrial planets and evolution of atmospheres.  

The author provides strong evidence from Venus's environment to show why exploration there poses difficulties yet remains important. Venus has an atmospheric pressure 90 times that of Earth along with surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead, conditions that would destroy any spacecraft within hours. However, as the article explains, Venus remains shrouded in mystery regarding its geological history and the mechanisms that led to runaway greenhouse warming. While harsh conditions persist today, understanding Venus's past may give insight into Earth's climate stability and cast light on Earth-sized exoplanets recently discovered in habitable zones of their stars. Gaining such knowledge through Venus exploration could help guide decisions around mitigating climate change back on Earth.

The challenges of Venus exploration are daunting yet surmountable according to the strategies the author outlines. Building on past Soviet lander missions that survived on the surface for brief periods, the article proposes that future landers could withstand conditions an hour or more through improved heat shields and automated science collection after touchdown. The author also advocates for an orbital mission mapping Venus's gravity and topography at multiple altitudes to identify geologically young surface features indicative of ongoing processes, gaining insights inaccessible through flybys. By utilizing multi-layered thermal protection, taking advantage of higher altitudes with less extreme environments, and automating tasks to minimize mission duration, the author makes a compelling case these strategies could enable productive Venus science despite serious risks.       

In conclusion, the author offers a well-reasoned argument that exploring Venus through proposed orbital and potential future surface missions is worth attempting in light of both the scientific value of unlocking the planet's mysteries and strategies to mitigate hazards. While Venus presents formidable dangers, as the article emphasizes, simply avoiding risks would come at the cost of knowledge. Gaining a fuller understanding of geological and atmospheric evolution using Venus as a case study could help answer questions central to exoplanet habitability and climate change back on Earth. For the potential scientific payoffs, facing the considerable challenges of exploring our closest planetary neighbor merits further consideration and efforts according to the case presented. The author persuasively argues the pursuit of Venus science, with prudent risk mitigation, represents a journey worth taking.

One of the most exciting and controversial technological advancements in recent years is the development of driverless cars. The article "Driverless Cars are Coming" raises several concerns about the safety, dependency, economic, and ethical implications of these vehicles. After carefully considering both sides of the argument, I believe that driverless cars are a step in the wrong direction.

Firstly, the safety concerns surrounding driverless cars are significant. As the article points out, traditional cars allow for human control, which embodies a sense of direct responsibility. However, with driverless cars, we are relying on sensors and algorithms to make life-or-death decisions. While manufacturers may promise advanced warning systems, these measures are not foolproof, and the risk of technical failure is always present. Furthermore, the introduction of driverless cars could lead to a disconnection from the act of driving and a lack of situational awareness. This could result in a decrease in overall safety, as drivers become too reliant on technology and neglect their own abilities.

Secondly, the increasing dependency on technology is a broader societal trend that driverless cars perpetuate. As we rely more and more on machines to perform tasks for us, we risk losing basic skills and awareness of our surroundings. The convenience of having a car drive itself could exacerbate this issue, leading to a society that is less aware and less capable of independent thought. This could have negative consequences in many areas of life, not just driving.

Thirdly, the economic and accessibility concerns surrounding driverless cars are significant. The cost of developing and owning such advanced technology could create a divide between those who can afford it and those who cannot. This could lead to wider socio-economic disparities and question the practicality of mass-producing vehicles that are not universally accessible.

Lastly, the legal and ethical challenges posed by driverless cars are complex and difficult to navigate. In the event of technology failure resulting in accidents, it is unclear who is responsible – the driver or the manufacturer. This grey area could lead to lengthy legal battles and moral dilemmas that could have been avoided altogether.

In conclusion, while the development of driverless cars represents a significant technological achievement, their adoption must be approached with caution. The safety, dependency, economic, and ethical concerns surrounding these vehicles are significant, and we must carefully consider the potential impacts on society, economy, and individual autonomy before embracing this technology. As a 10th grader, I believe that we should focus on developing safer and more accessible transportation options that do not sacrifice human independence and skill.

There are a number of things we can do to reduce our reliance on cars. One option is to carpool or take public transportation. This can help to reduce traffic congestion and pollution. Another option is to walk or bike. This is a great way to get exercise and fresh air. And finally, we can choose to live in communities that are designed for walking, biking, and public transportation.

And finally, it can make our communities more livable, as it creates a more walkable and biteable environment.

If we want to create a more sustainable future, we need to find ways to limit our reliance on cars. By carpooling, taking public transportation, walking, biking, and choosing to live in communities that are designed for walking, biking, and public transportation, we can make a difference.

Cell phones have become an essential tool for communication in our daily lives. However, when it comes to using them while driving, it's a topic of much debate. Some people argue that drivers should be able to use their cell phones in certain circumstances, while others believe that it's too risky and could lead to accidents. In my opinion, drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

Firstly, using a cell phone while driving is a major distraction. When we are behind the wheel, our focus should be on the road and the other cars around us. If we are busy texting, calling, or browsing social media, we are taking our eyes off the road and our hands off the wheel. This increases the chances of getting into an accident, which could not only harm us but also other innocent people. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, distracted driving was responsible for 3,166 deaths in the United States in 2017. This is a staggering number and proves that distracted driving is a serious issue that needs to be addressed.

Secondly, using a cell phone while driving impairs our reaction time. When we are driving, we need to be able to react quickly to unexpected situations. For example, if a pedestrian suddenly steps into the road, we need to be able to hit the brakes immediately. However, if we are busy with our cell phone, we might not be able to react as quickly, which could result in a tragic accident. Our reaction time is critical when it comes to driving, and using a cell phone compromises that.

Thirdly, there are many other ways to communicate while driving that are safer than using a cell phone. For example, we can use hands-free devices, such as Bluetooth headsets, to take calls and communicate with others. We can also use voice-to-text features to send messages or make calls without having to physically handle our phones. These alternatives allow us to communicate safely while still keeping our eyes on the road and our hands on the wheel.

Lastly, setting a good example is important. As drivers, we have a responsibility to set a good example for other drivers and pedestrians. If we use our cell phones while driving, we are sending a message that it's okay to do so, which could encourage other drivers to do the same. This could lead to a culture of distracted driving, which would be detrimental to road safety.

In conclusion, using a cell phone while driving is a risky behavior that can lead to accidents and fatalities. It's important that we prioritize road safety and avoid distractions while driving. There are safer alternatives available, such as hands-free devices and voice-to-text features, which allow us to communicate without compromising our safety. As drivers, we have a responsibility to set a good example and promote safe driving practices. Therefore, drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

Dear Florida Senator, I can't help but notice the controversy regarding the Electoral College and its role in electing the President of the United States. While most argue that the Electoral College is a violation of freedom, I strongly believe that the Electoral College promotes equality for the candidates and the people.

By using the Electoral College system, we create an equal playing field for the candidates. For example, The Electoral College system serves as "checksandbalances." In the words of the Office of the Federal Register in "What Is the Electoral College?": "The founding fathers established The Electoral College as a compromise between Congress and election of the President by a vote in Congress and election of the President by a popular vote of qualified citizens," Office of the Federal Register 1. This system of voting balances the voice of the people with the voice of Congress. Opposers might say that our votes don't even matter due to the fact that the popular vote doesn't directly determine our nation's President. This is far from reality, because the popular vote is vital to the Electoral College. The Office of the Federal Register writes that "most states have a winnertakeall system that awards all electors to the winning presidential candidate," Office of the Federal Register 7. This means that the popular vote does determine for most states anyway whether the candidate receives all the electoral votes for that particular state.

Not only does the Electoral College ensure equality for the candidates, but for the people as well. For example, in "The Indefensible Electoral College: Why even the best laid defenses of the system are wrong," Bradford Plume whines about how, "At the most basic level, the electoral college is unfair to voters," going on to say that, "Because of the winnertakeall system in each state, candidates don't spend time in states they know they have no chance of winning, focusing only on the tight races in the 'swing' states," Plume 13. However, Richard A. Poster makes a fair point: "The Electoral College requires a presidential candidate to have transregional appeal. No region South, Northeast, etc. has enough electoral votes to elect a president... If a candidate with only regional appeal becomes President the residents of the other regions are likely to feel disenfranchised to feel that their votes do not count, that the new president will have no regard for their interests, that he really isn't their president," Poster 19. Moreover, Poster also writes that "Voters in tossup states are more likely to pay close attention to the campaign to really listen to the competing candidates knowing that they are going to decide the election. They are likely to be the most thoughtful voters, on average...and the most thoughtful votes should be the ones to decide the election," Poster 20.

Overall, the Electoral College is a symbol of our freedom of speech. I do hope you take my thoughts under consideration. The Electoral College may be called "outdated." But as the saying goes, "If it 'ain't broke, don't fix it.

Advantages of Limiting Car Usage

Limiting car usage has numerous advantages that can positively impact both individuals and the environment. In recent years, there has been a growing trend to separate suburban life from auto use, and this movement, known as "smart planning", has shown great potential in improving overall quality of life and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. By limiting car usage, communities can become more compact, accessible, and environmentally friendly.

One of the main advantages of limiting car usage is the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. Cars are responsible for a significant percentage of these emissions, with passenger cars alone accounting for 12 percent in Europe and up to 50 percent in some car intensive areas in the United States. This is a huge impediment to efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and combat climate change. By limiting car usage and promoting alternative modes of transportation, such as walking, biking, and public transportation, communities can significantly decrease their carbon footprint.

Another advantage of limiting car usage is the improvement of overall air quality. In cities like Paris, where smog has become a major issue, partial driving bans have been enforced to clear the air. During these bans, congestion has decreased significantly and the levels of smog have reduced. This not only improves the health and wellbeing of the residents but also creates a more pleasant and livable environment. By limiting car usage, cities can combat air pollution and create cleaner and healthier spaces for their inhabitants.

Limiting car usage also has social and economic benefits. In the German suburb of Vauban, where residents have given up their cars, 70 percent of families do not own cars, and 57 percent sold a car to move into the community. This has created a more relaxed and stress free atmosphere, as residents no longer have to worry about the hassles of car ownership and the constant traffic congestion. Additionally, limiting car usage can promote more compact communities with walkable streets and accessible public transportation. Stores are placed closer to residential areas, making it more convenient for people to access essential services without having to rely on cars. This can have a positive impact on local businesses and economies.

In conclusion, limiting car usage has numerous advantages for individuals, communities, and the environment. By reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving air quality, and creating more compact and accessible communities, limiting car usage can help combat climate change, promote healthier living, and create more vibrant and livable spaces. It is an essential step towards creating a sustainable future.

The complex and controversial system of electing the President of the United States is undoubtedly at the heart of significant debate. For more than two centuries, the Electoral College has been a crucial component of this process. The debate on its relevance and efficacy has been an ongoing one. Many argue that it is outdated and should be replaced by a system based on popular vote, where the President-elect would be the winner of the highest number of votes from all eligible voters in the nation. This poses various challenges, but before taking a stance on either option, it's imperative to understand both systems' pros and cons, as well as their impact on the political landscape.

Proponents of the Electoral College maintain that it offers numerous advantages. Among these advantages are its historical significance, regional representation, protection against dictatorship, and a buffer to encourage greater compromise among politicians. Firstly, the Electoral College was established as an essential characteristic of the US Constitution in 1787. This system has been continually used over the years. It may be challenging to abandon it without fully considering its value as a long-standing tradition. Second, this system ensures that candidates are focused on achieving widespread support across regions, helping to minimize the concentration of campaigns in larger, more populous areas. Each state has a certain number of electors which is predetermined based on the sum of their representatives in Congress. This structure allows lesser populous states to have a stronger relative impact on the president's election, safeguarding the influence of the entirety of the United States' population.

Furthermore, the Electoral College serves as a backstop against the potential for dictatorial rulers or the emergence of "tyranny of the majority." By not directly electing the President by a simple majority of votes, there's a higher likelihood that the elected President will possess broader, more diverse support from the people. Despite popular vote systems in some other countries, the possibility of an extreme president being elected because of the temporary whims of a specific majority is diminished.

Lastly, it fosters a type of "bargaining" among political parties and legislators, ensuring a cooperative environment and giving candidates an incentive to establish bi-partisan collaborations. The winner-take-all results of a direct popular vote system could incentivize "winner-take-all" politics and diminish the importance of cooperation.

Nevertheless, the Electoral College system has its detractors who argue for its replacement with a more democratic system where the presidential election would be conducted through popular vote. Critics of the Electoral College contend that it can potentially lead to "swing states," where voter turnout is crucial in swaying elections. This discrepancy can lead to less significance being placed on the national implications of policies affecting all Americans, a situation which might be more fairly balanced via a direct popular vote system.

Another criticism involves the "winner takes all" approach employed by many states in the Electoral College process, where a state's electoral votes go to the person who won the popular vote overall in the state, even if they did not win a majority. This can lead to certain candidates receiving the electoral votes with less than a 50% majority, potentially going against the "will of the people," as evidenced in certain cases where the elected president won with minimal popular support. A direct popular vote would prevent these instances and ensure that the President would be the candidate with the majority of votes.

While addressing the challenges of both systems is essential, it must be acknowledged that there's no "perfect system" when dealing with the complex issues of voting and democracy. The Electoral College, as it exists today, might require improvements such as a gradual transition toward proportional allocation of electors, or establishing national popular voting primaries. Nevertheless, its benefits outweigh possible pitfalls, and by retaining this system while exploring potential reforms, we can better balance the challenges and advantages inherent in the Electoral College system.

In conclusion, while it's crucial to acknowledge the perspectives of those advocating for an election through popular vote, we should not discard the Electoral College system as outdated without considering its historical significance and potential benefits such as regional representation, the prevention of tyranny of the majority, and the fostering of greater political compromise. It's in our nation's best interest to work constructively to adapt the current system, taking into account its pitfalls, rather than wholly replace it with an incompletely thought-out alternative.

I look forward to continuing our conversation on the challenges and benefits of the Electoral College and the importance of democracy in this great country while we shape its future together. Please feel free to share your insights and opinions as well.

The author of "The Challenge of Exploring Venus" tries to explain the several complications of sending a mission to Venus. They provide tons of factual evidence about the geography and climate of Venus. They give many good points, but ultimately fail at their task to convince readers that Venus exploration is worth it. Along with a failed point, this author tends to go off on side-tangents that have minimal importance to the story.

"The Challenge of Exploring Venus" is an article about the positives and negatives of trying to land a spacecraft on Venus. He has a decent build-up into his first point while giving more and more small facts about our second planet. Venus is likely the most similar planet to Earth, with its rocky surface, hills, and mountains, but it has much more limiting factors to deter us from traveling there. It has terrible weather in comparison to Earth, with acidic carbon dioxide filling 97% of the atmosphere and with heats of 800 degrees Fahrenheit. The authors give plenty of information about this planet, most of it relevant to the topic at hand, and therefore succeeds in teaching you about Venus.

Even after succeeding in information given, the author fails to promote the idea that travel to Venus is worth all the cons. They write about NASA wanting to know as much as possible about one of our closest neighbors, but don't give enough reasons as to why it's worth it. With acidic atmospheres ripping through machinery, technologies don't stand a chance on the Venusian surface. With the science that we have, the most we can hope for is a jet-like experience, flying several miles above surface so that the pressure doesn't crush us instantly. Venus is additionally prone to constant volcanoes, earthquakes, and storms deadly enough to take out machinery. Given all this information, it seems like the author is trying to deter us from missions to Venus instead of promoting it, as they planned.

The final point to take into consideration when reading this article is the authors' side-tangents. Multiple times, the author delves into a side-topic as opposed to continuing on with the topic of Venus exploration. They start off the article with two sentences that have no relation to the story, yet confuse readers. The sentences are about Venus' nickname, the "Evening Star", and how even though it is a planet, it is still called this. This is completely irrelevant to exploration, as everyone knows it is a planet, and the "Evening Star" name is never mentioned again. Later on in the passage, the author rambles on about World War II-age computers and how they functioned properly even before the digital age. Once more, this is slightly irrelevant and does not contribute to the story at all except to add another paragraph instead of focusing on the specifics of how NASA is using them to help with Venus.

Overall, this article about Venus is less than "stellar". The author attempts to prove why Venus missions are a necessity, but doesn't quite get their point across. They provide great knowledge and information, despite being off-topic occasionally. This article is full of great facts, but the delivery is off and could have potentially been a better read if the author was on the other side of the argument, which has more proof to back it up. All in all, the author does not support their idea the best.

First impressions are incredibly powerful – often an opinion formed in a matter of moments can remain unchanged for our entire lives. This is because humans make biased decisions in order to quickly and effectively evaluate a situation. The introduction of a new person to a situation often requires rapid assessment and so we tend to make a snap judgement almost instantly. We then use this first impression as a basis for all our future opinions of this person. This bias makes it difficult for us to take the time to evolve our impression, even if our initial assessment was wrong. 

For example, people who always dress formally are often assumed to be stuffy or conservative. However, this first impression may not match up with their true personality in reality. Instead of taking the time to get to know them on a deeper level, we often remain stuck in this first impression and thus, never quite accurately gauging who this person truly is. 

Another example is in the workplace. An employee who performs a task poorly in the beginning may be seen as incompetent, regardless of if their performance improves over time. This is a form of bias known as the ‘halo effect’ – our first impression sets the stage for all future interactions and it is difficult to depart from that. 

It is clear why it is so difficult to change a first impression – often it requires more effort than people are willing to give in order for them to understand who a person actually is. We lean more towards taking the path of least resistance, and when it comes to changing our opinion, that means staying with our first impression. It is not impossible to change of course, but it is a difficult feat, and one which should be done with caution.

In this modern era of easy access to technology, children are heavily influenced by the electronic world into which they immerse themselves. Thus, the younger generations are growing more familiar and comfortable with technology than their own parents and grandparents will ever be. In well-endowed school districts, students often have Chromebooks, Macs, or another brand of a small, portable laptop. It becomes easier to teach students with online material when each and every child has his or her own school-issued device, and other schools have gone as far as to implement distance-learning, a form of education offered through the accessibility of technology. Distance-learning, while heavily reliant on electricity and technology, is greatly beneficial to students because it would both allow those who are not able to attend school due to sickness and reach those who live far away from a learning institution.

Sickness spreads easily in a crowded, public environment where many tools, like pencils, scissors, and desks are shared. Students often cannot afford to miss school due to illness, so they will attend anyway, no matter the severity of their sickness. Even with the addition of laptops into education, missing a day of learning has the potential to impact student learning because he or she is not present for the teacher's lecture and explanation of material. Through distance-learning, students who are sick would be able to connect with the class and teacher in real-time and be able to ask questions to further his or her understanding. If the student was in the hospital, having come down with a more serious illness, like pneumonia, he or she would likely miss out on a few concepts from class but later video chat with a teacher while simultaneously not missing out on medical attention.

Students who live far away from their school would also benefit from in-home learning. Those who live in more rural parts of a school district often have an early wake-up call for a long commute riddled with morning rush-hour traffic. Then, in school, the student is already mentally exhausted and must prepare for the long trek home. Distance learning would eliminate the commute for faraway students, saving them money in gasoline and time in transit. They would also not need to wake up as early and go to bed as late, allowing for a healthier sleep schedule. Many students take part in before- or after-school activites, like a sport. Elite swimmers practice before the sun comes up each morning, hurry off to school for a few hours of learning, then head back to the pool for a second practice or weight routine. Balancing athletics, school, and sleep can prove difficult, especially during end-of-season competitions that run during school days or weeks. But with distance-learning, student-athletes would be able to catch up on missed work while they were absent and have the oppurtunity to ask their teachers questions when they return.

However, distance-learning is not a perfect solution; it sets up a heavy dependence on electricity and wireless connectivity. In times of inclement weather, like a thunderstorm, high winds, or heavy ice, power lines can be knocked out, disconnecting students reliant on their laptop to learn. While inclement weather always carries with it the chance of a school cancellation, some school districts are more prepared for such catastrophes. For example, Minnesota and New York are often slammed with horrendous snowstorms that bring several feet of snow, but these northern states come prepared, bringing their snowplows out in full force and working around the clock to ensure that the roads are safe. Students who live in areas of extreme temperatures and weather are prepared to brave the dangers of the outside. So, students learning from remote areas will then be missing out because are unable to learn, while those physically in school will continue on unaffected. Furthermore, learning at home can prove difficult for those who find it hard to focus. Going to school provides a different, somewhat unfamiliar environment in which students are not constantly distracted by everything. At home, the television, fridge, and bed can all take students' focus from learning. Students who decide to learn from home ought to be dedicated, keep themselves engaged in their virtual classrooms, and able to ignore the pulls of the soft bed with fluffy pillows and the fridge with its store of delicious food.

Distance-learning will provide another option for students who are otherwise unable to learn in the traditional classroom setting. It will be not for the lazy but rather the driven, responsible, and committed, since not everyone possesses the level of focus required to drown out the sounds of distraction. Technology has become easy to use and relatively inexpensive, and as a result, it has introduced options that previously did not exist. In the world of education, techonology will increase the quality of learning for those everywhere.
